 3                SENATOR KENNEDY:   Thank you very 

 4   much, Mr. President.  

 5                I rise today to honor the remarkable 

 6   life of Jesse Edward Nash, Jr., who passed away 

 7   on May 11th at the age of 90.  

 8                Mr. President, imagine for a second 

 9   that it's 1965 at Canisius College in Buffalo, 

10   New York.  The student body and a small 

11   population of African-American students are 

12   looking to change the world around them, starting 

13   with the lack of leadership positions for 

14   African-American students.  These students had 

15   grit, they had a message, they had energy -- all 

16   they needed was a mentor to guide them.  And they 

17   found this and more in a first-year sociology 

18   professor, Jesse Edward Nash, Jr., who helped 

19   them found the Afro-American Society, seeking 

20   constructive ways to advance civil rights.

21                That was Jesse Nash, always seeking 

22   constructive change to the people and communities 

23   around him.  Frustrated with the lack of 

24   advancement for inner-city residents, Mr. Nash 

25   took action by serving as the executive director 


                                                                3397

 1   of the Model Cities agency from 1967 to 1971.  

 2   Disappointed with the lack of healthcare access 

 3   on Buffalo's east side, Mr. Nash worked 

 4   tirelessly to establish a health center in 1972, 

 5   which has since been dedicated in his name.  

 6   Noticing a lack of academic research in 

 7   African-American studies, Mr. Nash focused his 

 8   career on urban power structures and their effect 

 9   on the black community.

10                You see, Mr. Jesse Nash, Jr., came 

11   from a family of doers.  His father, the Reverend 

12   Jesse Edward Nash, Sr., was a long-time pastor of 

13   the Michigan Avenue Baptist Church in Buffalo, 

14   helping to bring branches of the Urban League and 

15   NAACP to Buffalo.  His mother, Frances Jackson 

16   Nash, was the solid rock, helping his father help 

17   all people throughout his life.  

18                Jesse Nash, Jr., followed in his 

19   parents' footsteps, seeking ways to give back.  

20   He founded Seventy-Eight Restoration, focused on 

21   community development, and created the Emerson 

22   Row apartments for low-income individuals.  

23   Mr. Nash spearheaded the Buffalo Waterfront 

24   Alternatives Study, the War Memorial Stadium 

25   Restoration Project, and the Erie Community 


                                                                3398

 1   College City Campus feasibility study.

 2                Among civic groups, Mr. Nash was a 

 3   member of Alpha Sigma Nu, the Jesuit National 

 4   Honor Society, Omega Psi Phi, a lifetime member 

 5   of the NAACP, and vice president of the Buffalo 

 6   Urban League.  

 7                And as a professor concerned with 

 8   education and health access, he gave back through 

 9   service on the College Council of SUNY Buffalo 

10   State, the New York State Commission on 

11   Minorities in Health-Related Professions in 

12   Higher Education, as well as on the boards of 

13   Child and Family Services, the Millard Fillmore 

14   Gates Hospital, and the Erie County Industrial 

15   Development Agency.

16                Mr. Nash is survived by his wife of 

17   65 years, Hortense Nash; two sons, George Raymond 

18   Nash and Jesse Edward Nash, III; and one 

19   daughter, Deborah Nash Franklin.

20                Jesse Edward Nash, Jr., it was clear 

21   from his first year as a professor as Canisius 

22   that he would do great things.  Over his life he 

23   showed that determination and grit, combined with 

24   kindness and being a gentle soul.  He 

25   demonstrated that with these traits, an 


                                                                3399

 1   individual can go very far in life and have a 

 2   resounding impact on his or her community.

 3                Buffalo and New York thank Jesse 

 4   Edward Nash, Jr., for a lifetime of commitment to 

 5   Buffalo, New York State, and this great nation.  

 6   His example will be revered for generations to 

 7   come.  

 8                Mr. President, thank you for your 

 9   indulgence.  And I would ask that the honor of 

10   the house be given to the Nash family at this 

11   time.  Thank you very much.

 8                ACTING PRESIDENT GRIFFO:   Senator

10                SENATOR HAMILTON:   Mr. President, I 

11   rise to salute the past, present and ongoing 

12   contributions of the Caribbean-American community 

13   to New York and in recognition of June as 

14   Caribbean Heritage Month.

15                We take this moment to honor our 

16   intertwined history with the Caribbean since 

17   New York was New Amsterdam.  Caribbean 

18   immigration didn't start in the 20th century -- 

19   it is essential to the founding, and foundations, 

20   of this country.  

21                There is certainly no shortage of 

22   distinguished Caribbean-Americans to name:  

23   Founding Father Alexander Hamilton, former 

24   Secretary of State Colin Powell, actor and singer 

25   Harry Belafonte, basketball star Patrick Ewing, 


                                                                3406

 1   former U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder, actor 

 2   Sidney Poitier, and the late Congresswoman 

 3   Shirley Chisholm.  

 4                And I will not neglect those whose 

 5   names are not bold-faced in the papers, those 

 6   people in our history who did not migrate 

 7   voluntarily, and people whose jobs are behind the 

 8   scenes, those who have been scientists, 

 9   inventors, caretakers, transit workers or 

10   secretaries -- just a few of the jobs we don't 

11   take the time to recognize often enough.

12                Caribbean-Americans have worked in 

13   all sectors that make New York State the capital 

14   of the world.  Through generations, we have built 

15   family and community.  Those families include my 

16   own.  

17                My 101-year-old great-uncle Robby 

18   Tate is still alive today, who migrated to 

19   New York City from St. Thomas Parish in Barbados 

20   with my great-grandparents.  They continued to 

21   share stories with my family about our rich 

22   Caribbean history.  Growing up as a 

23   third-generation Barbadian, they taught me the 

24   value of hard work and advocating for the people.  

25   My uncle served our country bravely in the U.S. 


                                                                3407

 1   Army through our country's most difficult times.  

 2                Caribbean immigrants have been 

 3   contributing to the well-being of American 

 4   society since its founding.  During 

 5   Caribbean-American Heritage Month, we honor the 

 6   courage and perseverance of the 

 7   Caribbean-American community.  Families with 

 8   roots in the Caribbean like mine, and millions 

 9   across the state, pursued the American dream, 

10   sharing the immigrant story held in common with 

11   countless millions of fellow Americans.  I take 

12   this moment to honor them and their sacrifice.

13                Often overlooked in the immigrant 

14   experience is the propensity to overcome 

15   barriers.  The barriers may relate to language -- 

16   Spanish and French being among the languages 

17   Caribbean-Americans can lay claim to -- culture 

18   shock, a difference in the pace or cold weather, 

19   and navigating one's way far from home, without 

20   family and familiarity.  

21                Despite those challenges, these 

22   generations of migrants and their 

23   Caribbean-American descendants persisted, 

24   persevered, and created the largest Caribbean 

25   population outside the Caribbean here in 


                                                                3408

 1   New York -- a vibrant and impactful 

 2   representation that enriches our economy and 

 3   institutions and communities.
